text: Every build pulls in dependencies you didn't write and probably haven't read. A software bill of materials is how you keep track of exactly what's in there, in a format a machine can query later. We'll look at what a real SBOM records, the two formats you'll actually encounter, how to generate one and scan it for known issues, and why having this inventory ready before an incident changes how fast you can answer one question: are we affected?

An SBOM records the exact name and version of every component, direct and transitive, not a loose range. It records the supplier, the license, and a package URL — a standardized identifier like pkg colon pypi slash requests at 2.31.0 — so tooling can match it unambiguously. And it records relationships: which component pulled in which dependency underneath it. What it doesn't record is a verdict. An SBOM is an inventory, not a scan result.

Two formats dominate real tooling. SPDX started as a license-compliance format and is now an ISO and IEC standard, common anywhere license tracking matters most. CycloneDX, from OWASP, was built security-first, with native support for vulnerability data and component relationships. Neither has displaced the other — syft, a common generator, can emit either one, and which you produce often comes down to what a downstream consumer or customer requires.

The inventory becomes useful once you feed it to a scanner. Grype takes an SBOM and matches every component's package URL against vulnerability databases, reporting severity for anything with known issues. Run it in CI on every build, and on a schedule against existing builds too, so a vulnerability disclosed after the fact in a dependency you haven't touched in months still gets caught the next time the scan runs.

Here's where it pays off. When a disclosure comes out about a widely used library, the question is always the same: are we affected. Without an SBOM, that means grepping lockfiles across every repository by hand, under pressure, likely missing a transitive dependency three layers deep. With SBOMs already generated and stored centrally for every build, it's a query — does any artifact contain this package at this version. Minutes, not days.

An SBOM plus a scanner turns a supply chain question into something you can answer on demand instead of scrambling to reconstruct. Last lesson in this chapter pulls everything together: secrets scanning, least privilege, and SBOMs into one concrete checklist you run through before any pipeline ships to production.
